Towel
tow'el
n. (a cloth for wiping; in the Gospel, the servant's linen Christ girded Himself with)
Old French toaille, from a Germanic root meaning to wash. Twice in Scripture, both in one paragraph of John 13, and the object is a badge of office — the office of a slave.

Biblical Definition

John records the towel twice in two verses, and the deliberateness of the account is the point. “He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself” (Joh 13:4). Then: “After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded” (Joh 13:5). Every clause is a deliberate act — rose, laid aside, took, girded, poured, began to wash, wiped. In that household the foot-washing was the work of the lowest slave present, and there was none, and no disciple would volunteer; so the Lord of glory put on the badge of the office. John has already told us He did it knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands, which makes the act an expression of His authority rather than a suspension of it. And He binds it on His church: “If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet” (Joh 13:14). The towel is the visible form of the great self-emptying: He “made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant” (Php 2:7).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines towel as a cloth used for wiping the hands and for other purposes.

expand to see more

TOW'EL, n. [Fr. touaille; It. tovaglia.]

A cloth used for wiping the hands and for other purposes.

Took a towel and girded himself. John 13.

Towel of state, a long napkin formerly used at table.

The word is of Germanic origin, from a root signifying to wash.

Key Scripture

John 13:4 — "He riseth from supper, and laid aside his garments; and took a towel, and girded himself."

John 13:5 — "After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples' feet, and to wipe them with the towel wherewith he was girded."

John 13:14 — "If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another's feet."

Philippians 2:7 — "But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men:"

Modern Corruption

Servant language has become the standard vocabulary of Christian leadership while the towel itself is rarely picked up.

expand to see more

No word is more common in contemporary ministry than servant, and few acts are rarer than the one John describes. The corruption is not hypocrisy exactly; it is the substitution of a posture for a task. A servant-leader conference, a servant-leader title, a platform from which servanthood is taught — John 13 offers none of these. It offers a specific job that nobody in the room wanted, done by the one man with the most right to refuse. The test the passage supplies is unglamorous and local: is there a task in this congregation that the senior man will actually do because no one else will?

There is also a sacramental corruption running the other way. Some traditions have made foot-washing a third ordinance, and while the practice can be edifying, the New Testament nowhere treats it as the church ordained it treats baptism and the Supper. The Reformed position keeps the commanded ordinances two and keeps John 13:14 as a binding command about the manner of life among brethren rather than a rite. Ritualizing the towel is one more way of not using it, since a ceremony once a year is easier than a habit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek lention (G3012), a linen cloth, towel; diazonnumi (G1241), to gird about; niptar, basin; Latin linteum, linen.

expand to see more

Greek lention (G3012) — a linen towel, borrowed from Latin linteum; John 13:4-5, and nowhere else in the New Testament.

Greek diezosen heauton (G1241) — He girded Himself; the same verb used of a slave's working dress.

Greek nipter (G3537) — the basin; also found only here in the New Testament.

Greek morphen doulou (G3444, G1401) — the form of a slave; Philippians 2:7, the doctrine the towel enacts.

Greek ekenosen (G2758) — He emptied Himself; the same verse, and the ground of the whole scene.

Usage

"“Took a towel, and girded himself” — the badge of the lowest slave in the house."

"“Ye also ought to wash one another's feet” — a manner of life, not a rite."

"“Took upon him the form of a servant” — the towel is that doctrine made visible."
